History:
- Chief complaint: Soreness and cracking skin of the hands, primarily palms; dryness noted elsewhere (legs) but milder.
- Onset and duration: Symptoms began about 3–4 months ago and have progressively worsened.
- Course and context: Palms are very dry, cracked, and itchy with occasional bleeding from scratching. Wearing gloves irregularly during cleaning work as a hotel housekeeper; recently changed job ~4 months ago. Symptoms impair ability to work; recently had 3 days off.
- Associated/negative symptoms: No fever, nausea, vomiting, bowel or urinary symptoms; appetite and general wellbeing preserved.
- Triggers/relief: Likely exposure to cleaning products with inconsistent glove use; OTC moisturizers (E45) and antihistamines provided no relief.

Past Medical History:
- Diabetes mellitus type 2; on metformin.
- No known allergies.
- No prior diagnosed skin disease reported.

Medications:
- Metformin (dose/route/frequency not documented).

Allergies:
- No known drug or other allergies documented.

Family/Social History:
- Family history notable for diabetes.
- Works as a hotel housekeeper; sometimes does not wear gloves; non-smoker; alcohol use a couple of pints per week.

Physical Examination:
- Palms: very cracked, dry, and itchy; scratching associated with minor bleeding.
- Legs: dryness present but less severe.
- Systemic signs: No fever; patient otherwise well; no other acute abnormalities described.
- Not recorded: Additional vital signs or full exam details.

Impression:
- Primary: Irritant contact dermatitis of the hands (palms), likely related to occupational exposure to cleaning products and inconsistent glove use.
- Differential diagnoses considered (consistent with transcript and plan): Allergic contact dermatitis; hand dermatitis/eczema; xerosis with diabetic-related dryness. (Conflict noted: none.)

Management Plan:
- Protective measures: Wear gloves at all times when cleaning; minimize exposure to irritants.
- Pharmacologic therapy: Begin topical corticosteroid cream for inflammation; use stronger emollients (moisturizers) applied 3–4 times daily to improve skin hydration; continue for the next 1–2 weeks.
- Follow-up: Reassess in 1–2 weeks; sooner if worsening, spreading, or no improvement.
- Additional steps: Prescription to be sent to patient’s pharmacy. If not improved after 1–2 weeks, consider alternative/adjunctive therapies and potential patch testing for allergic contact dermatitis.

Patient Summary:
- Laura Parkinson, a 45-year-old hotel housekeeper with diabetes, presents with several months of dry, cracked, itchy palms, worsened with work-related irritants. Plan includes protective gloves, topical steroids, and frequent moisturizers with a follow-up in 1–2 weeks. A prescription will be sent to the pharmacy.

Key Takeaways:
- Use gloves consistently during cleaning to reduce irritant exposure.
- Apply topical corticosteroid as prescribed and moisturize the hands frequently (3–4 times daily).
- Return for follow-up in 1–2 weeks or sooner if symptoms worsen or spread.

Next Steps:
- Pick up prescribed topical corticosteroid and emollients from the pharmacy.
- Maintain glove use and monitor response over 1–2 weeks; consider patch testing if no improvement.
- If symptoms worsen or you notice spreading, return sooner for re-evaluation.
